Complement

/KOM-pluh-ment/ · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Complement means to complete or make perfect by adding something that was lacking.

The tart cranberry sauce complements the rich turkey, supplying exactly the sharpness the dish was missing.

Worked Example

A defender who reads the game perfectly can complement a striker who lives to attack; together they form the spine of a whole team.

The defender doesn't just play alongside the striker — his strengths fill exactly the gaps in the striker's game, completing the pairing. That completing-by-filling-a-gap idea is precisely what complement means.

How Strong Is It? — match → complete → complement

match vs. complement

match vs. complement: Two colors can simply match; a scarf that complements an outfit actively supplies what the look was missing.

complete vs. complement

complete vs. complement: To complement something is to fill its gap; to complete it is to leave nothing missing at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — com-

Prefix — com-: together, completely

Root — ple-

Root — ple-: to fill (Latin plere)

Suffix — -ment

Suffix — -ment: result or process of

Put it together

Put it together: Com- (completely) + ple- (to fill) + -ment (result): the thing that fills something up completely. As a verb, to complement is to supply exactly what was missing so the whole becomes perfect.

Use the root in a new word: replete

Use the root in a new word: replete: The museum's archive is replete with sketches, letters, and unfinished drafts.

Root Check

Word Choice

Everyday & academic — spelling trap

Don't confuse this with COMPLIMENT (a polite expression of praise). Remember: complEment with an E completes something — a sauce complements a dish, and two angles that add up to 90 degrees are complementary. If you mean kind words of praise, you want complIment with an I. Complement also works as a noun: 'The scarf is the perfect complement to her coat.'
